title: The first medical X-ray showed a hand wearing a ring: Röntgen's wife's, in December 1895
body: On **8 November 1895** Wilhelm Röntgen, working in Würzburg, noticed a faint glow on a screen while experimenting with a cathode-ray tube and realised he had found an unknown kind of ray, which he labelled X, the mathematical symbol for an unknown. About six weeks later he made the first medical X-ray image: his wife Anna Bertha Ludwig's hand, with her ring showing as a dark blob on a finger of bones. On seeing her own skeleton she reportedly said that she had seen her death. Röntgen refused to patent the discovery so that everyone could benefit, and in 1901 he received the first Nobel Prize in Physics.

cover.alt: The first medical X-ray, a sepia print of the bones of a hand with a dark ring on one finger, labelled in handwriting 'Hand mit Ringen'

slides.prompt: What did Anna Bertha Ludwig reportedly exclaim when she saw the X-ray of her own hand?
slides.detail: The image, made about six weeks after the discovery, showed the bones of her hand and her ring. It is regarded as the first medical X-ray.

slides.heading: From a faint glow to a Nobel Prize

First medical X-ray: his wife's hand
He X-rays the anatomist Albert von Kölliker's hand

slides.question: Why are they called X-rays?
options: They were made with an X-shaped tube
slides.explanation: Röntgen first just called them rays, then X-rays, using X as the mathematical symbol for an unknown quantity. In German and several other languages they are named after him instead.

slides.alt: A black-and-white studio portrait of Wilhelm Röntgen, a man with a full dark beard wearing a suit and waistcoat
slides.caption: Wilhelm Röntgen around 1900. He refused to patent X-rays, wanting society as a whole to benefit, and received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901.

slides.heading: Why bones show up
slides.text: X-rays are electromagnetic radiation with far shorter wavelengths than visible light. Dense tissue such as bone absorbs more of them than soft tissue does, so bones and metal rings cast shadows on a photographic plate placed behind the body.
